seoDescription: Learn how to use LangChain to query CSV and Excel files using natural language with OpenAI models. This tutorial covers loading datasets (CSV/Excel), using the LangChain CSV agent and a Python REPL tool to run pandas operations, constructing prompts, reducing hallucination with temperature=0, handling prompt-injection risks, and practical examples like counting rows, filtering by gender or tenure, and converting Excel to CSV for analysis.

chapters.title: Introduction and dataset overview
chapters.description: Introduces the goal—using LangChain to query CSV and Excel files via natural language—and the Black Friday Sales dataset used for examples.

chapters.title: Why use the CSV agent and security considerations
chapters.description: Explains the LangChain CSV agent, how it runs a Python agent under the hood, and warns about prompt injection and environment trust.

chapters.title: Creating the CSV agent and model settings
chapters.description: Shows the imports, agent creation with OpenAI LLM, and rationale for settings like temperature=0 and verbose mode.

chapters.title: Agent internals: chains, prompts, and scratch pad
chapters.description: Inspects the agent structure: language model chains, prompts, the pandas DataFrame context, the Python REPL tool, and the scratch pad concept.

chapters.title: Prompt structure and demonstration: counting rows
chapters.description: Reviews the agent prompt details (df name, tools, output format) and demonstrates a simple query to count rows using the Python REPL.

chapters.title: Agent workflow and example queries
chapters.description: Walks through agent thought/action/observation cycle and demonstrates queries: total rows, counting females, filtering by years stayed, and combined filters.

chapters.title: Custom loaders, Excel handling, and limitations
chapters.description: Explains using custom CSV loaders, converting Excel to CSV for LangChain, and limitations of treating spreadsheets as DataFrames rather than spreadsheets with cell formulas.

chapters.title: Excel examples, ratio queries, and closing
chapters.description: Demonstrates Excel-based examples (column names, average age, most frequent country, male-to-female ratio), and concludes with use cases and final remarks.

summary:
## Key Concepts

- **LangChain CSV Agent**: Uses a Python agent and a **python REPL** tool to run pandas operations on loaded CSV data and respond to natural language queries.

- **OpenAI LLM Integration**: Provide an **OpenAI API key** and pass an LLM into the agent. Set **temperature=0** to reduce hallucination when returning factual data from CSV/Excel.

- **Prompt & Context**: The agent receives a prompt that defines the DataFrame name (`df`), available tools, and expected output format. The head of the DataFrame is included so the model can infer column names and values.

- **Scratch Pad / Chaining**: The agent uses a **scratch pad** to carry intermediate outputs (actions, observations) between model calls, enabling multi-step reasoning like counting and filtering.

- **Examples & Queries**:
  - Count rows (length of DataFrame).
  - Count categorical values (e.g., gender where values are `f`/`m`).
  - Filter numeric ranges (e.g., stay in current city > 3 years).
  - Combine filters (e.g., female and stayed > 3 years).
  - Aggregate queries (e.g., most frequent country, average age, male-to-female ratio).

> [!TIP] Use verbose mode during development to inspect prompts and the agent's thought/action/observation sequence.

> [!NOTE] LangChain lacks native Excel import; convert Excel to CSV or load into a pandas DataFrame before passing to the agent.

> [!IMPORTANT] Because the CSV agent executes Python code, guard against prompt injection and untrusted user input by controlling the execution environment.

## Takeaways

- Treat spreadsheets as **DataFrames**: the agent operates on DataFrame semantics (columns, rows, pandas queries), not spreadsheet-specific features like cell formulas.
- The approach enables building simple apps that let non-pandas users query tabular data with natural language, while giving you options to extend with custom loaders and chains.
